utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. No preliminaries, therefore we'll continue. We were informed, Ms. MacGregor, that you expect to finish your cross-examination in the first session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bukva.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bukva, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given yesterday at the beginning of your testimony, that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Ms. MacGregor will now continue her cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Bukva. I see that you don't have a copy of your statement in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I don't know if the Defence has a copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If you'd like one, I am going to ask you a couple of questions referring to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: I'm going to be asking you about paragraphs 34 and 35 of your statement about the Vaso Miskin incident on 27 May 1992. I see that you've opened the statement. Now according to your statement, the information obtained by you and your service showed that Mirza Jamakovic planted an explosive device in a building across from the bread kiosk. Who was your source for that information?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source for that information was only one. It was a prewar operative source that I had.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of that source?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because I - how shall I say? - inherited it under a pseudonym and not a name and surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You knew the source by a pseudonym, is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You also state that Muslim authorities attempted to liquidate Jamakovic and that he lost his hand in the explosion that occurred when they attempted to kill him. When did you learn about that incident?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Considering that this incident was an extreme interest, it caused an important reaction among the international community. The Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska ordered that this incident be thoroughly investigated because the VRS was, of course, blamed for what had happened in Vase Miskina Street.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: If I can --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My service --

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: -- stop you. I believe when you're talking about this incident in your answer that you're referring to the initial Vaso Miskin incident. My question is: When did you learn about the explosion that resulted in Jamakovic losing his hand?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, I didn't understand. I just wanted to say that we worked on this case intensively. And the first information, the one I mentioned in the statement, we'd received perhaps two or three months after the Vaso Miskin incident. So if it happened on the 27th May, three months later we already had this information, roughly. I cannot be precise. If it happened in the end of May, we had this information sometime towards the end of August.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And then when did you learn about the incident where Jamakovic lost his hand?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just explained. The information that he lost his hand I received perhaps three months after the Vaso Miskin incident. Now when he lost his hand, on which date, when the assassination attempt took place, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: You state that his son was killed by a sniper after that because Jamakovic would not stop talking about the Vaso Miskin incident. When did you learnt about the death of his son?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was later. Later. In another contact with that source when he called from the city. I don't know exactly when, but it was later. I cannot pin-point a date because it all happened 22 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: And when you said "contact with that source," are you referring to the same source with the pseudonym that you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. It's the same source but it was a different contact, a different occasion when he made contact and let me know about the death of Jamakovic's son.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. MacGregor, should we spend a lot of time on paragraph 34 and 35 where it's deprived of any facts. If I read, for example, that the son was allegedly killed by a Chetnik sniper. "The boy was killed at the place where it was absolutely impossible to hit by infantry weapons from the VRS positions." We don't even know where he was, so there is no way to test this evidence and for that reason the probative value is close to zero. The Defence should be aware of that, but apparently they are insufficiently aware of that. And to cross-examine in detail, and I know that you didn't use this line, but paragraph 34 and 35 is, "We received information which shows," what's the information, how does it show? We all know by now that it took Trial Chambers in this Tribunal up to weeks or months to establish the details of an explosion of -- it's totally useless. And if the Defence isn't aware of that, then that's no reason for the Prosecution then in cross-examination to just join the Defence in considering this to be evidence which assists the Chamber. I hope, of course, that both parties will become aware of that. What we see from these paragraphs is that some information reached a witness on which he based some conclusions. That's all. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Can I please have 65 ter 31143.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Colonel Bukva, as we wait for this to load on the screen, this is a request dated 19 January 1993 in which Major Dusan Savcic requests the use of 20 Muslims to fortify the front line position at Zlatiste. Do you have a chance to see that on the screen in front of you? Perhaps if the B/C/S version was a bit larger, it may be easier for you to see. I draw your attention to the bottom left to the handwritten approval signed by Colonel Lugonja. Are you able to see that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Did Colonel Lugonja's authority include the work assignments of Muslim detainees?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Remand prisons and prisons were in the jurisdiction of the command, the garrison command. In this case it's just an approval, and here in this case we read, "I give consent," which doesn't mean that he approved it. Only the garrison command could approve it. Colonel Lugonja did not have such powers. He was only consulted by the command and this is proof. He only says that he agrees. He gives his consent, whereas the decision was in the hands of the command.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your interpretation is different than our English translation, so perhaps the Defence and the Prosecution can consult if we feel there is a significant difference. Colonel Bukva, in English the translation reads: "I approve the engagement of the detainees," and you've read that as "I give consent." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Serbian version that I'm reading, in the lower left corner it says: "I agree that prisoners be engaged in works" or "I give consent." "I agree" or "give consent." And then he signs it, Colonel Lugonja.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask one additional question. That's the handwritten portion. Now, the document itself, and I read is addressed to Lugonja, Lugonja, and the Chief of Staff writes: "We are requesting that you let us temporarily use 20 Muslims on the 19th of January ..." There is a request that Mr. Lugonja let the Chief of Staff, the command of the 1st Romanija Infantry Brigade use detainees. That is clearly asking for a decision, for approval, for consent, whatever you want to call it, but the document, the request clearly indicates that Savcic needs a decision by Lugonja that he allows this to happen or that he let them use those detainees. Would you agree with me that that's the gist of this request?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree with you. And that's exactly what's written here, "I give consent." But I emphasize the second part of the answer, but the right to approve these prisoners was in the exclusive jurisdiction of the command. So Colonel Lugonja was not able to order how the prisoners would be used. He could only say, "I do not agree," and then the commander would not allow it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So using those prisoners was dependent on the consent, agreement, even if not ordered but at least was dependent on the consent of Lugonja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it didn't have to be exclusively dependent on his consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person who actually decided just wanted to hear --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I stop you. You add a word to what I said, "exclusively." If you change my words, it's of no use to answer my questions. I said they could be used dependent on the consent and, of course, if Savcic would want that as well, and it's clear from this request that he does so. Any further comment on the matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Generally speaking I agree with you, but if you allow I can add that situations like this were rare.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was rare that this was allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not seeking that kind of information. I've one other question for you. Do you think it legitimate to use detainees to work on the front line in -- to make fortifications? Or would that be illegal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that in this specific case, these prisoners were not exposed to enemy fire from the other side in this specific case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I -- stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Their engagement was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't asking you whether they were exposed to enemy fire. I put a general question to you whether it's legal to use prisoners to -- for fortification works at the front line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that's defined anywhere in the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I couldn't give you an exact answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. MacGregor.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to tender 65 ter 31143 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31143 receives number P6709, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'd also like for the record to draw the attention to the evidence already in the record on the Vaso Miskin incident and what happened to Jamakovic. And that's the evidence of Ekrem Suljevic, including P889, e-court page 11, paragraph 66 and 67; and also an investigative report of the incident in which his son was killed at P1106. And the Prosecution has no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. MacGregor. Mr. Lukic, any questions in re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I might have only one on this Jamakovic, 34 and 35, from this gentleman's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bukva, good morning again. Do you remember that I put it to you that Jamakovic's son died in a mine explosion? When we were talking.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I talked about what I knew about it, I believe you mentioned something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 35 of your statement, you say allegedly from a Chetnik sniper. That is the information as you received it.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD BUKVA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said I received that information from an operative source on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't have any further questions either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Bukva -- well, I may take it that the re-examination has not triggered any further need for questions by the Prosecution. Mr. Bukva, this concludes your testimony in this court. I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague, for having answered the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the next witness be kept standby. I'd like to briefly move into private session only for a very short moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And we are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session. I filled the screen a little bit now so that the curtains can be opened more quickly. Mr. Lukic, you said the witness was not yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I doubt that he is here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you suggested we take the break first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll do so, and perhaps then we take the break --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then no need for the break --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has arrived. Then could the witness be escorted into the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. MACGREGOR
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I take this opportunity to ask for permission to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but under one condition: That you open the second curtain as well. Thank you so much, Ms. MacGregor. You are excused. Apparently, Mr. Lukic, Mr. Mladic wants to consult with you. Mr. Lukic, you -- is there anything that needs our attention --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Something was taken from General Mladic and he would like to have it back, but I think it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know what was --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- maybe better to discuss --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- taken from him --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's a pin, one pin, a tie pin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe for security reasons that -- and it will be returned to him, I take it. Further details to be dealt with. Good morning, Mr. Indjic. I saw that the first thing you did was to greet the accused. That's not commonly done in this courtroom. You appear before a Court. Would you please refrain from any communications even not verbally with the accused. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Is text is handed out to you now. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Indjic. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just as a preliminary, I wanted to notify the Chamber of two things. The first thing being that I believe in terms of my cross estimate, I'll be an hour less in time at least. And the second thing, I just wanted to notify the Chamber that the witness did receive a Rule 90(E) caution previously during his testimony and we believe he should receive it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you know the approach of the Chamber, that not knowing what questions will be put to the witness, that we leave it to the parties whether it's appropriate to request the Chamber to give a 90(E) warning. Mr. Stojanovic. Mr. Indjic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find Mr. Stojanovic to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I just may ask before I begin to have the usher take the summaries of the witness statements that we need to provide to the interpreters, because I did not manage to do that before I begin. I was short of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, you were taken by surprise. That's understandable under the present situation. Please proceed. Your request is granted and the summaries will be distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Indjic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, could you please slowly speak your name out and your last name.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: My name is Milenko Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, did you provide a statement to General Mladic's Defence, a written statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see document 65 ter number 1D01759. I don't know if we need to wait for the usher before we get the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, on the left-hand side of the screen you see the B/C/S version and on the right-hand side the English version of your statement. My question to you is the following: Is the signature on the front page of this signature [as interpreted] precisely your signature?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will put the same question to you. Is the signature on this page that you have in front of you your signature and is the date that is written there written by your very own hand?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you that I put when you provided the statement and after you have spoken the solemn declaration in the courtroom today, would the answers to my questions be identical as the answers you provided in your statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the witness's statement with the 65 ter number 1D01759.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D01759 receives number D614, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Stojanovic, if the witness confirmation says something about the number of pages, it sometime would be good to fill in the number of pages. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honours. Thank you. With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to read the summary of the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness Milenko Indjic, with the forming of the UNPROFOR mission in 1992 in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, pursuant to an order of the then Federal Secretary for National Defence, was appointed as liaison officer of the JNA in the group for co-operation with UNPROFOR. With the establishment of the Army of Republika Srpska, in view of the fact that he lived in Sarajevo, he continued to carry out said duties in Republika Srpska and he remained at that duty practically until the end of the war. He testified to the situation in Sarajevo before the war broke out in 1992, about the arming and organising of Muslim paramilitary forces, and about the blockade of Yugoslav People's Army barracks in Sarajevo. After handing over the control over Sarajevo airport, which passed from VRS hands to the UNPROFOR, he personally was aware of the abuse of the mutual agreement and that the airport was used for the military needs of the Muslim side, which is reflected in weapons and ammunition supplies and enabling the Muslim military and civil leadership to use the airport without any obstacles for their own needs. He took part in most of the cease-fire negotiations and witnesses the abuse of signed cease-fires by the B and H Army. He asserts that he personally knew that the reports by military observers about the number of shells fired around Sarajevo is not accurate because the data about that was received from the warring parties and were frequently used for media manipulation. As liaison officer, he personally attended a large number of meetings which were attended by General Mladic as well, and he testified to the position and to the character of General Mladic as well as his relationship towards the participants in the negotiations. Finally, in his statement he notes that the UNPROFOR went beyond its mandate before the NATO bombing of the positions of the VRS, and he talked about the reasons why the order was issued to place them under control, disarm them, and take away their communications means. He is personally aware and will testify about the position of the VRS towards these persons and the status and the treatment they had while they were under the control of the VRS. And now I would like the put some questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Stojanovic, there is some guidance. Having read the statement, having heard the summary of the statement, I would urge you to focus on facts rather than on opinion. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now again look at paragraph 14 of the witness statement, which is now D614, if I understood correctly and noted it down correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you have your statement in front of you. I would like to ask you for a clarification of a part of your statement where you say UNPROFOR allowed the tunnel to be built under the airport, which was primarily used for the regrouping of military forces and its other purpose, and then you continue. My question is: Did you have any personal knowledge about the work by the ABiH Army to dig a tunnel under the airport runway?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: During a certain period, I personally received aerial photographs from UNPROFOR of the Sarajevo airport where it was written in French that they were confidential, and the position of the entrance to the tunnel was marked on them, the direction of the tunnel, and the exit from the tunnel. These photographs I handed over to the defence attorneys in the trial of General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you mind to answer the question. The question was whether you have any personal knowledge about the work done by the ABiH Army to dig the tunnel. So that is the army being involved in digging the tunnel. Your answer may be -- contain very interesting information but it is not an answer to the question. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer to the question in the form that you have now put it is that I don't have any personal knowledge about the digging of the tunnel, but I do have personal knowledge about the existence of the tunnel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there is no dispute about the existence of the tunnel, is there? So therefore, we don't have to deal with that. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: At any point in time during the work to dig the tunnel and after the tunnel was dug, did the VRS lodge any protests about the tunnel with UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: After we received clear data that the tunnel existed, every meeting of the corps commander with representatives of UNPROFOR also dealt with that part where representatives of UNPROFOR were requested to shut down the tunnel and prevent the regrouping of Muslim forces. These protests would usually receive the following answer, that we were making things up and that the tunnel did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you personally present at any of the meetings when the aerial photographs were discussed that you mentioned earlier?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I was present at a meeting at the corps command between General Galic and the then commander of UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo, General Soubirou. After the protests stated by General Galic about the tunnel, General Soubirou warned us with a laugh that we should not be making things up about something that did not exist. I asked General Galic for permission to bring the aerial photographs so that we could show them to General Soubirou. When I brought these photographs, I asked - and I must say I did it in a provocative way - I asked General Soubirou to help us to understand what was written on the photographs, because it was written in French, to which he got up very angry and left the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at paragraph 16 of your statement. In B/C/S at one point we'll have to move to the next page. I'll say when.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Indjic, you say in paragraph 16: "Observing the agreed cease-fires, the Serb side suffered large losses because the Muslims would always breach the agreement ..." Now let's move to the next page in B/C/S. "... by opening fire or by performing engineering works to fix their positions." And then the last sentence: "In the Sarajevo theatre of war, the Muslim forces took more territory by digging in the periods of cease-fire than by all their combat activities throughout the war." My question is: What did you mean by "they took territory by digging during cease-fires"?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: From the very beginning of the war, I believe there were posters all over Sarajevo under Muslim control saying, "We can dig our way to victory." By digging during cease-fires, the Muslims were trying to advance their positions by carrying out engineering works in such a way as to occupy the space between confrontation lines, knowing that the Serbs wouldn't open fire at them during cease-fires. We had huge problems to explain to UNPROFOR that engineering works also constitute a violation of the cease-fire agreement and movements of positions also constitute a violation. We had to stop our soldiers from opening fire when they saw that the enemy is advancing on them, coming closer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These violations of the cease-fire by one signatory to the agreement, did they lead to any protests to the UNPROFOR from your side?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: On many occasions, at different levels, we warned the UNPROFOR and brought to their attention the breaches of the cease-fire agreement through engineering works. I have to explain to you one essential feature of Serbs. The Serbs are very reluctant to complain, protest, and ask somebody else to defend them. They usually defend themselves. But it was our obligation to warn the UNPROFOR of what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we call up 65 ter 1D04175. Page 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, this is one of the documents that the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps on the 19th of February, 1994, sent to the Main Staff. Could you please look at item 1, which says: [As read] "Engineering works continued at Mojmilo towards Sucura ... houses and the SVC Barracks towards the Jewish Cemetery to Bosut and the Osmica from Sucura houses towards Nedzarici towards Energoinvest from Dzemala Bijedic Street and in the sector of Sugreb (Mount Igman)." My question is: Are these engineering works precisely what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: That is what I meant. At item 1 of the regular combat reports from corps to the Main Staff usually contains information about the enemy, such is the format of the report. So in every period of cease-fire you can analyse through regular combat reports, looking at item 1, you can analyse what was going on on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful if the two documents could be enlarged a bit. The letters are very small. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at paragraph 3. It says under subheading "Situation on the ground," UNPROFOR activities. And the text below reads: "A meeting was held in Lukavica between General Galic and General Soubirou. The following chief problems were identified ..." And then it goes on to say: [As read] "The Muslims continue to violate the cease-fire agreement by carrying out engineering works and opening fire at our positions (Hadzici)." My question is: These complaints and protests lodged by the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps to UNPROFOR over violations of the cease-fire, were they verbal or written?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Both. It was possible to warn the UNPROFOR verbally or in writing if no meetings had been scheduled and there was important information to impart to UNPROFOR. We could always tell them about something important. It was not necessary. It was not required to write a report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: These meetings between the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and high-ranking UNPROFOR officers, did they require your presence as the liaison officer in the logistics of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: In the preparation and organisation of the meeting, somebody from the group in charge of co-operation with international organisations had to be present. If I was physically there, it was usually myself. And if I was away, then somebody from my group would be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I tender 65 ter 1D04175.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4175 receives number D615, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness, we'll take a break. Therefore, would you please follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the question came to my mind to what extent most of what you dealt with is in dispute, that is, that complaints were lodged, meetings were held, the existence of the tunnel seems not to be in dispute. Even we have heard quite some evidence through various, even Prosecution witnesses, on the matter, so I wonder to what extent it's repetitive and I wonder to what extent it is a matter of dispute. Would you please keep that in mind, especially if you ask for more time than you indicated before. We take a break and will resume at 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be brought in. The Chamber was informed that Mr. Mladic had difficulties with the tie pin. It is exclusively a security matter. Security matters are within the competence of the Registry; therefore, the Chamber will not deal with it because it has no impact whatsoever on the court proceedings. Therefore, we leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I kindly ask that we call up the following document in e-court, 65 ter 1D04157. I would likely us to focus on paragraph 8. Let's just briefly stay on page 1 to see what this document is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, it's again a regular combat report from the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps dated 4 March 1994. Now focus on paragraph 8. It says in the subheading, "Conclusions, forecasts, decisions": [As read] "The Muslims are still carrying out engineering works at their positions digging trenches (roads) towards our positions, in order to achieve the most favourable ... position possible in relation to our forces. Despite regular warnings and protests sent to UNPROFOR observers, the latter are unable to prevent the enemy's activities completely which results in certain soldiers and commanding officers being tempted to open fire even without the approval of their superior command." I would like to ask you: Was this behaviour on the part of the enemy something that constituted their obligations and a violation of the cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It was as much a violation of the cease-fire agreement as if they had opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tender 1D04157.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4157 receives number D616, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let us see another document, 65 ter 1D04159.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, this is a record of a meeting at the Sarajevo airport with what the author described as the Chetnik side. The command of the 1st Corps of the BH Army made this report on 1st of January, 1995. And it says that from the aggressor side there were Colonel Cedo Sladoje, as Chief of Staff of the SRK, and you as the liaison officer. General Gobillard opens the meeting, presents the main points, and then Colonel Sladoje says: I have been informed by my scouts that our agreement has not been observed, has not been honoured. When what we agreed has been done, then I will sit down here. General Gobillard responds: My scouts inform me that the agreement has not been fulfilled. And he says also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- in a way you have the right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One moment, please. Can we go to the next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: General Gobillard says: [As read] "In a way you are right, but the DMZ shall be honoured. We will tell you what has been withdrawn and what was not." Will you please tell the Court what this meeting discussed and what problem did Colonel Sladoje emphasize?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I remember this meeting. At this meeting we were supposed to identify to what degree the agreement on the demilitarisation of Mount Igman and Mount Bjelasnica had been implemented. What is important is that this meeting was held in January 1995, while the agreement on demilitarisation was signed in the second half of 1993. From the record of this meeting, it is evident that Muslim forces had not fully withdrawn from the demilitarised zone. That's what these three letters mean, DMZ. Which means that over the course of 18 months, the agreement failed to be implemented. And it speaks volumes about the way the Muslim forces treated such agreements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, on page 25, lines 20 to 21, you are recorded as having said: "General Gobillard responds: My scouts informed me that the agreement has not been fulfilled." I think that there must have been a mistake on your part. These are the words that Mr. Sladoje used --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- not Mr. Gobillard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those are the words of Colonel Sladoje. Thank you very much for your assistance. I tender this record dated 5 January 1995, 65 ter number 1D04159.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D4159 receives number D617, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Weber, is there any dispute about the Muslim side not, certainly not in every respect, meeting their obligations under the DMZ agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe the evidence stands for itself. We've received a lot of evidence about the activities of both sides during the course of the agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- so I would not encapsulate it in one simple sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, but I didn't ask you whether there was a dispute about whether the Serbs did but at least the Muslims, not to say -- doesn't say anything about the Serbs. Mr. Stojanovic, you are asking for more time and apparently you are -- you are eliciting evidence which -- on a matter which is not in dispute. And we have followed the proceedings carefully. I mean, it came to my mind because we have heard evidence about it before, so therefore use the remaining five minutes preferably on matters which are in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with all due respect, over the break we tried to clarify this with the Prosecution. We asked if we could stipulate these questions. And as far as I understood the position of the Prosecution, yes, the Muslim side did do some engineering works, but in the view of the Prosecution that would not constitute a violation of the cease-fire. This is why we put this question. The other thing is that, prompted by your digression from yesterday's transcript, page 25039, lines 17 to 22, where you said and suggested that in view of the fact that the statement of this witness was quite general, the Chamber would like to know who violated the cease-fire so that the other side could check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't say anything about the testimony -- I didn't say anything about the testimony of this witness yesterday, as far as I remember. And I don't see this document to deal with engineering works. That was the previous document, if I remember well. And, Mr. Weber, did you -- were you approached for a stipulation?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, and what I actually believed I informed Mr. Lukic was that if he would like to write facts, not conclusions, down, I'd be happy to look at it. And so, you know, I need to -- what is the -- not a conclusion but the Prosecution would actually like a fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- that could be reviewed and then read into the record. So I'm going to look at that. I think that would be our standard approach and -- instead of just oral on record conversations with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- obscure facts, things of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We should avoid that observations as I just made take more time than -- and the parties are again encouraged to agree on what is in dispute and what is not in dispute. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we now look at D614 in e-court again, please. This is the witness's statement. And I would like to direct your attention to paragraph 19 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question regarding the explanation of your statement on this matter, Mr. Indjic, is you said that it was established that fire was opened at the centre of Sarajevo from Muslim positions. So now I'm asking you if you had any knowledge about civilian buildings or facilities in Sarajevo or some other buildings in Sarajevo were being used as locations where artillery positions of the 1st Corps of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army were placed.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I'm a little bit confused. Paragraph 19 refers to a very specific matter. As for this second question, it's not related to paragraph 19. I can respond to both. I can answer in relation to paragraph 19 and then to this second part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to go step by step. So first regarding paragraph 19, you say it was established in that period that fire was opened at the centre of Sarajevo, in parentheses, in the area of Higijenski Zavod. So I'm asking you who established this fact, that the shelling in the area of the public health institute had come from the Muslim positions.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: All right. In view of a series of manipulations that accompany every war, including the one in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in view of the high level of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- professional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- qualifications of the British cadre --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I stop you there. The simple question was who established the fact that fire was opened at the centre of Sarajevo, who did that. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Clear, clear, clear. The UNPROFOR command headed by General Rose, thanks to the artillery radar posted, the Cymbeline radar, established -- without any doubt established that the trajectory of the mines which hit the public health institute indicated that they were fired from Muslim positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before you continue, of course the Chamber -- apart from what exactly the relevance is that the other party did perhaps something wrong as well. The relevant question would be what attack, is there any report, and what do these reports say. That's, of course, for the Chamber to give weight to that -- this evidence, would like to have that kind of information. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have information about certain civilian facilities or military facilities were being used as positions of the 1st Corps of the B and H Army and for artillery fire in their immediate vicinity?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: There was a lot of information. If we set out from the fact that the 1st Corps was deployed in Sarajevo, the 1st Corps of the Muslim army, which had 11 brigades, that the establishment was taken over from the former JNA, and it's a three-fold organisation, and that each brigade had three battalions, that each battalion had three companies, that the area of responsibility of one company was 1 to 2 kilometres wide, the positions of companies in Sarajevo demanded an area of 150 square kilometres, and the width of Sarajevo from the west on is 15 kilometres. That means that 10 lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'm stopping you again. You give a long explanation as to why, apparently, you think that there is a basis for perhaps an answer to the question. I do not know where it all ends. The simple question was: Do you have information about certain civilian facilities or military facilities were being used as positions of the 1st Corps? Could you tell us whether you have such information and then what that is. Not why but what.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, this is precisely what I wanted to say. There are about 200 different sorts of command posts in Sarajevo which were mostly located in civilian facilities; specifically, I personally, in the month of August in 1992, when it was already war, went to have a coffee with the commander of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sefer Halilovic, at his command, so that I personally know that his command was located in the cellar of a civilian building of the city assembly in the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, apparently we move now to a different subject. The source of fire established by Cymbeline radar, that where I said that what we would be interested in, you moved apparently to a different subject, and therefore I take it that you don't have that information or that you don't consider it important enough to bring it to our attention, which, of course, makes the previous answers of the witness -- it does not strengthen their probative value.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, then I would just put one question to Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you say that the British members of UNPROFOR established thanks to radar observation of what the location was from where the artillery shell was fired that hit the public health institute. Did you see that information or a report in a letter of UNPROFOR? Did you see a written form of that report?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see that report in writing, but from British officers that I was in contact with, I got that information from them, and I know that General Rose went to see Silajdzic to lodge a strong protest about what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Date of that shell being fired was? A time. When was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that this was in 1993, before Alija Izetbegovic left for Washington to a meeting at which the lifting of the weapons embargo imposed on the Muslim side was supposed to be lifted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That gives a rough time-frame. Mr. Stojanovic, where the witness is able to tell us that General Rose lodged a strong protest, I take it that is recorded somewhere, which is usually done. Have you explored that to see whether what the witness tells us is also reflected in any such report?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are working on it, Your Honour, and I hope that we will be able to identify that by the end of the examination of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You interviewed the witness so it comes as a bit of a surprise that it's only now that you are working on it. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And I'm going to end with one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at paragraph 27 of your statement, please, where you talk about the situation. This is in the middle of the paragraph. The situation when members of UNPROFOR who were in the territory controlled by the VRS were placed under their control and their communications devices and weapons were taken from them. The people that you talk about in your statement, where were they specifically located?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the French contingent of UNPROFOR which was billeted in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps area in Lukavica, and their task was to monitor heavy weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your best recollection, how many members of French UNPROFOR were placed under the control of the VRS on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I think it was about 25 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And in which building did they continue to sojourn physically after they were placed under VRS control?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: They remained in the same building in the same premises that they were in until then, only the weapons and their communication means were placed in a different room which was then locked.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And what was the way that these members of the French contingent were treated in terms of food, accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The members of UNPROFOR were treated professionally. They were not abused. The only thing was that they were not permitted to move outside of the premises where they were being kept.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, thank you very much. I don't have any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, again, we've heard quite a bit of evidence of UNPROFOR members being deprived of their liberty. Could you tell us what you told us now about the 25, approximately, where were they kept, so that we are able to link your information with other evidence we've seen? I've got no idea, if you say they stayed in the same premises, what premises you are talking about. What premises did they stay in where they had been before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if you look at my earlier answer, is that -- where it states that they were in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps area of responsibility, so they were right next to the building where the command of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps was. They were literally some 50 to 100 metres away from the location of the corps HQ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you aware of any other UNPROFOR members that were deprived of their liberty in the zone of the corps which were not allowed to stay in the same premises where they had been before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The answer to that question would be only about what I heard later. I did not know about anything about other members of UNPROFOR, about them being taken in, so I don't have any personal information about that. I don't have personal knowledge about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even not as a liaison officer you were not privy with that information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And what you later heard, from whom did you hear it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In conversations at the command while making reports about how many members of the international forces there were and at which locations. There was a record kept and that was submitted as part of combat reports about the situation on the ground, how many members of UNPROFOR were there and in which locations. That is to say, I personally did not take part or have any personal knowledge about this except in relation to this particular group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do I understand that in the corps command a record was kept of where UNPROFOR members who were not free to move any further, were deprived of their liberty, where they were kept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that was part of the -- this was reported to the corps command by the lower units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we come to the domain of what I think what was there. Again, I think that that's how it was, but I don't have any personal insight regarding those reports, meaning the reports of subordinate units to their command. I did see a collective report which was sent to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: One short follow-up question in relation to this matter. In paragraph 27 of your statement, you refer to an order to place under control and disarm the UNPROFOR members in the territory controlled by the VRS. Who issued that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember that day very well. I was in my office when the deputy operations officer came and conveyed the order from the Main Staff that members of UNPROFOR were to be placed under control and separated from their weapons and communication devices. He emphasized that strict care must be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- taken, that not a single member of UNPROFOR should be hurt in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: An order from the Main Staff. Was it a written order or a verbal order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. The duty operations officer could have received an oral or a written order, and I got that order from the duty operations officer of the corps command in -- orally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know who personally at the Main Staff issued this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you say "Main Staff," you refer to the Main Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Weber, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You'll find him to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And just so -- I think you even clarified it, but for the record, is it correct that you speak the English language?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still, but not so well as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just leaving off -- just picking up where we just left off, are the events that you were -- that you were describing to the Judges about the UNPROFOR members being held pursuant to an order of the VRS Main Staff, does that relate to events that occurred on the 26th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I mentioned in my statement and I repeat now that I am not able to speak in any competent way about dates because I have a problem with dates. I can say that these events began with the NATO air strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll come back to the topic. How about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could pick up also, since we were just looking at the statement on the screen, with D614. I just have some basic questions about paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of your statement, you state: "When the UNPROFOR mission was established in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, I was assigned pursuant to the order of the Federal Secretary for National Defence to the position of liaison officer within the group for co-operation with UNPROFOR ..." Simple question: When was this order received by you, the approximate date?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It could have been February or March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In this paragraph you indicate that the group at the time was headed by General Aksentijevic. Is it correct that this group was under the command of the 2nd Military District at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was linked to the 2nd Military District organisationally, but the reports went directly to the Federal Secretary for National Defence. So I think it was only logistically linked to the 2nd Military District and organisationally they were related directly to the Federal Secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for that clarification. Up until September 1992, you were based in the PTT building in Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it was September but it was the second half of 1992. I think it was September or the end of August, then September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. During the remainder of the war you were based in the Lukavica barracks at the headquarters of the SRK; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It couldn't be the SRK or the Main Staff. It was the command of the SRK, the same building where my office was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In Lukavica, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: In Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of the second paragraph of your statement, you indicate that you ended your service with the rank of lieutenant-colonel. Is it correct that you were promoted to this rank during the war at the beginning of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It's correct that I was promoted during the war, and it was an early promotion, I think six months earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You understood my next question. It was an accelerated promotion; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It was not fast-track or accelerated. It was just early. There are different categories of promotion. This one was early.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Moving on away from your statement, is it correct that contacts with representatives of the international community went through your office in Lukavica?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Among other things at the office in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your primary task was to receive requests, protests, and petitions from representatives of the international community addressed to Bosnian Serb institutions. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be better to say that the main task was mediating in the communication between various institutions and the institutions of the Serbian side, because that part of the job that you mentioned, receiving requests and protests, et cetera, was only one part of our job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Since you provided a little slightly different answer, I would like to look at your Karadzic statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 31179, page 17 in e-court. It's paragraph 56.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we meanwhile ask the witness to tell us what he meant when he said "mediating in the communication between various institutions." Various institutions of what, of the international community or UNPROFOR or the ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Institutions of the international community, UNPROFOR, International Red Cross, UNHCR, international press, warring parties, everybody who needed to make contact with the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That included the Muslim armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I -- if you'll indulge me a little bit more on that topic, I was going to go into that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, before you is your Karadzic statement. And I'd like to direct your -- I believe it's only on one side. And I'll read it out. I don't know if you can read paragraph 56 for yourself. It stated: "The primary task that the group performed was receiving requests, protests, and possessions from the other side or representatives of the international community for institutions on our side." This was your statement for the Karadzic case; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Nothing is in issue. I just expanded a little what was said, very briefly. Only in essential features. I clarified what this was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Is it correct that you processed these requests or protests and forwarded them to the relevant individual or institution?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The part of the question where you said "processed" or "treated" is not clear. I cannot answer. As for forwarded, forwarding to the addressee, to those for whom it was intended, that part is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, let's go back to your Karadzic statement that's on the screen before us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Next paragraph, 57.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So I'm using your words: "We processed these requests, or rather what we received, and forwarded them to the relevant institutions ... and vice versa, replies and requests from our side for one of these institutions." So when you say "processed," are you saying that you received requests and you then forwarded them to the relevant institution?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I understand what is meant in this statement. For instance, if a protest was sent, especially in the beginning, in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: -- when we didn't have translation services --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to keep a little organised. We'll go through specific examples, but I understand your answer as yes, that that was an accurate statement, that you forwarded the requests to the relevant institutions and vice versa. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. What --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I want to say what is meant by "processed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, what we have on our screen now, did we receive that in e-court or -- because I have some difficulties in --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- getting --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- the 65 ter I have is 31179.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still have in e-court a nine-page document, whereas we are supposed to be on page 17. Now I have the right one, I think. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been fixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just want --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Judge, Your Honour, I believe that the witness is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- trying to get your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one thing. The document I have in e-court before me is in English. English is not my native tongue. I have some knowledge, but I don't understand it perfectly. And since it is important here to be precise, I would like the document to be shown to me in my native tongue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be no B/C/S version of this document. If --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the Karadzic statement which we have signed from the witness, and we do not -- Ms. Stewart is checking again but -- oh, we don't have a B/C/S version of the -- this statement from the Karadzic case. From the Karadzic Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But Mr. Weber read the relevant part into the transcript and it was interpreted to the witness. And the witness was going to explain what he meant by "we processed these requests."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we can't assist you. The portions read to you are interpreted for you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. And thank you, Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe that where we left off was you wanted to make a comment about what you meant by the word "processed these requests." If you could just please give us a very brief explanation as to what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: In the early days, it happened sometimes that a document that was to be sent out by us to UNPROFOR needed to be translated and sent to UNPROFOR in English and vice versa. The documents received from certain organisations would arrive in English and then we would translate them and forward them, pass them on. That's what I meant to say. I, nor anybody else in my group, did not have the right to process anything in the sense of changing the content or the essence of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to try to stay on track here, but you've introduced a -- a temporal element. Did that stay the same throughout the remainder of the war, that your group did not have the right to process anything in the sense of changes to the content or essence of the document?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Right. We were allowed in no way to change the content or the gist of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I want to go step by step here and just go through very particular organisations and how things were communicated. So if you could please just listen to my questions. Is it correct that you received requests and protests from the United Nations, including UNPROFOR, UNMOs, and UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to the -- these requests and protests related to UN institutions, would they be made orally and in writing to you?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I want to be emphatic about one thing. Your question reads would they be made to me. I said we forwarded protests to the addressee. They could be verbal or written. In fact, they were both verbal and written. But they were not sent to me. I am not the addressee of these protests, Milenko Indjic or anybody else from the group in charge of co-operation with international organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, that's fair and that's well understood that you were forwarding them and I'm sorry if I introduced any confusion, but let's move on. Is it also correct that you received and forwarded requests and protest letters from the ECMM? I believe you already mentioned the ICRC and other nongovernmental organisations.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the ECMM's mandate had already finished when the VRS was established. So they didn't even exist anymore. But as for the ICRC and nongovernmental organisations, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the protest letters received by your liaison offices were passed on to your superiors in the chain of command of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: They were forwarded to the addressees. If they were addressed to the command of the corps, they were sent to the corps command. If they were addressed to the Main Staff, we passed them on to the Main Staff. The situation became a little easier in 1993 when UNPROFOR established their own liaison office at Pale. So the bulk of communication addressed to the Main Staff went through that office and not my liaison office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If you received an oral request or protest directed to General Mladic, how would you communicate that to the General?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: If it concerned something that was not confidential, then a telephone call would be made to General Mladic or the duty officer, or it would be included in a regular report in writing. If something required a degree of confidentiality, then we made every effort to convey the message to General Mladic in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You just mentioned "or the duty officer." Of which level of command are you referring to the duty officer of?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The duty officer at the command of the Main Staff. My explanation about confidentiality was meant to explain also that all communications that we used were not secure and they could not be used for passing on confidential information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was just reminded that it might be break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take the break. The witness may follow the usher. We'd like to see you back, Mr. Indjic, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll wait for the witness to enter the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, since we have your Karadzic statement on the screen, I just wanted to go to one other paragraph in it before we resume with the topic we were discussing. In paragraph 58 of your Karadzic statement, it indicates that you stated: "The work of liaison officers precludes any possibility of independent decision-making ... as a liaison officer, I'm in a position to propose the solution to a problem ... but I can't decide on the solution." Is that an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do I understand correctly from that that you had no independent authority to decide how to respond to a protest or a request in your position as a liaison officer? You had to respond according to how you were instructed from your superiors.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I had to reply in accordance with the response of the person or the institution to whom the protest was addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's a more broad statement. Specifically, if it was addressed to General Mladic and General Mladic told you how to respond, you were bound by those instructions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I've never had a case where I would receive directly from General Mladic my instructions as to how to respond. The protests that were addressed to Pale received replies from the Main Staff always in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll go through some examples, and I'll revisit this. Since you were a member of the SRK command, how would you inform General Galic or General Milosevic of the protests you received?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: If the protest was in writing, I would hand it to him. If it was a verbal protest, I would pass it on to the commander or, if the commander was away, then to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And you followed that procedure during both the time of General Galic and General Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: That was the standard procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Would the protests ever be discussed at the morning SRK command meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: In the period when I attended morning briefings, the meetings did not discuss protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that all protests that were directed to a higher level of command were also forwarded to the level of command that the protest referred to? To give you an example, if a protest regarding VRS activities in Sarajevo was sent to a member of the Main Staff, would that protest also be forwarded to the SRK commander?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot answer that question. I don't know whether that was a rule for those who were sending the protests. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at one of your previous statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31180, page 51.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, Mr. Indjic, is it correct that you provided an interview or you sat for an interview with the Office of the Prosecutor in April of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It's correct that I had an interview with Barry Hogan, the investigator, but I cannot recall the date. I do know that it was Barry Hogan. The surname was entered incorrectly. It's Hogan. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to an answer that you provided during the course of this interview which is in the middle of the page. I'll read it to you. Your answer was: "In principle, I can say that all protests that arrived at the higher level were also forwarded to the level that the protest referred to. And together with that, if necessary, the protests were accompanied by corresponding orders from the higher level to the lower level on what to do further." Sir, that is what you told Investigator Hogan; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Excellent. And you are in the right place, and if you read carefully what is written here, you can see that it was not the protest from UNPROFOR that would be sent to two different levels but it would -- if it were sent to the higher level, then that higher level would pass it down to the lower level, the part that referred to the lower level, with some sort of adequate order about what had to be done in respect of that protest.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the commander of the SRK, whether it was General Galic or General Milosevic, that they would be informed of the details of a protest even if the protest letter was not directly to them?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know the answer to that question. What the communication was between the corps commander and the chief of the Main Staff and his assistant, I can't answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
