utterances.text: If we could please zoom out on this page. I'll come back to it. And I'll find -- I'm sorry, Your Honours. Thank you for your patience. I don't have the specific point in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And I'll come right back to that, sir. Is it correct that you received and forwarded requests or complaints from other Bosnian Serb institutions to members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. Serbs lodging protests with Serbs? It's not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you receive any protests from Bosnian Serb institutions to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I never saw a protest like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you not only had to deal with liaison duties for the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps but you also had to deal with liaison duties for the other corps and units and sometimes even political entities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: The most precise answer would be that I was working on duties of liaison officer for all those who needed to contact anyone in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps sector, because the bulk of political and military negotiations took place in the neutral zone of the Sarajevo airport. As for this specific question, I did not carry out liaison officer duties for other corps, but frequently I was engaged in organising various meetings of the political leadership.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: While we have the interview in front of us, could we go to page 6. And actually, if we could go on to the next page, to page 7. There it is at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, during your interview, the question posed to you through the interpreter was: "And if I've understood correctly, this means that your duties were not only liaison duties relating to the Romanija-Sarajevo Corps, but also to all other corps and units, including even political sides, contacts?" Your answer was: "Er, in a large number of cases." Is that what you said during your interview?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I probably did because that's what it says there, but what I meant was going beyond the confines of the Romanija-Sarajevo Corps because I worked as a liaison officer for the main corps, some political, civilian authorities, but I didn't work for other corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, I understand that you were assigned to the SRK, but do you understand my questions relate to your function as a liaison officer and that you would receive protests and transmit requests relayed to the other corps as well. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No, I did not receive requests relating to other corps because there was a liaison officer office at the main corps. Other corps also had their own liaison officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could just go back to the earlier reference that I was seeking to have. It's page 53 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the meantime, I would like to clarify one word. In your last answer, Mr. Indjic, at least that was the interpretation, you said: "... because there was a liaison officer office at the main corps." What do you mean by "main corps"? If it correctly represents what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not main corps. Main Staff. The Main Staff in Han Pijesak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, I'd now like to take you to a question that was posed through the interpreter as -- it's at the bottom of the page in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could please have it enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's -- the question was: "However, as you said earlier, er, after the protests were filed, they would be forwarded to General Galic and there would be no reason for him not to have been aware of the filed protests." Your answer was recorded as: "There would be no reason. Only if, if he was not physically" present "there at the moment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You added the word "present."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Oh, thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. I'll just re-read it just so it's clear on the record what the answer was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "There would be no reason. Only if, if he was not physically there at the moment." That was what you said during your interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was just right now just seeking to confirm your previous statement, and you've done that. Thank you. During the war, can you approximate how many protests you received from UNPROFOR and other international entities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It's not very wise to make approximate conclusions because then you would held to that, so I would rather avoid giving any approximate evaluations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that it was a large number of protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, what one considers large, a large number, is considered by another a small number. So could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was -- I'm not -- I hear you and I was thinking along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How frequently would you receive, let's start with, written protests?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: That all depended on the combat situation on the ground, if there was fierce fighting underway or not, so that again is a relative thing. They would come as needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you able to give any type of approximate -- approximation of how frequently you would receive protests orally? Every day, every week, every two weeks, once a year?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Sometimes it would be every day, sometimes it would be once a month. It all depended on the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you received protests for both small and big incidents? And what I mean by that, I mean small day-to-day events, and big meaning events that were being, let's say, widely covered in the media?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I cannot answer that question because it's absolutely imprecise. I don't know what you consider a small, what you consider a big incident. We could say that the death of one person is a small incident, the death of five people could be considered a big incident. So I really don't know how to answer unless you put a more specific question to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's very fair. Did you get -- some of the protest letters that you received concerned shelling of specific areas of Sarajevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot answer the question. It's still a very general question. I don't know if there was such protests or not. It's such a general question that I really cannot answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could go to, actually, then, your prior transcript based on that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's the Galic transcript, which is uploaded under 65 ter 31178. I ask that it not be broadcast. I ask that it not be broadcast. Your Honour, I would note that this was in private session during the Galic proceedings. I've asked for the transcript right now to be not broadcast. I think that I could safely read the portion that I'm seeking to elicit. It's on page 50 of that transcript. However, if you'd like, I'd be happy to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we're not in private session, I think the transcript will be public.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I asked for it not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whatever you read --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document still on the screen shouldn't be broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Oh, yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It should be removed from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think still the portion on the transcript is readable from the public gallery, so therefore we usually wait for one or two minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole Prosecution team seems to be struggling with the details of the technicalities of the curtains up or down. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just let us know if we need to assist at all since we're here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, I'd like to now discuss with you some specific aspects of your relationship with General Mladic. Is it correct that you had over 100 conversations with General Mladic during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Again, that would be an approximation. There were a lot of conversations during meetings that were conducted, conversations at the command post. I don't know how many of them happened. I really couldn't say that with any kind of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your Karadzic testimony, on multiple occasions you responded to answers by saying that things were "one of a hundred conversations I had during the war with General Mladic as liaison officer."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is on Karadzic transcript page 32605.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Also on that page, you said: "I said a little bit earlier that I spoke with General Mladic at least a hundred times." So do you agree that that's at least an accurate statement, that you spoke with General Mladic at least a hundred times during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I agree that I gave this statement in the Karadzic case, and I regret giving it because these are approximate numbers. And I see that everything that is said in an approximate way you are taking as a fact, and I regret giving that statement. However, I did give it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just asking if you said things and if you feel that they should be corrected, please let us know. And I think it's clear that -- that you were giving an approximate -- an approximation of at least something on a previous occasion. I'd like to move on. Did you -- did General Mladic ever call you during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that he asked for me personally. It's possible, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall any occasion where there was a phone call and you were brought to the phone and on the other line was General Mladic during the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Now you have reminded me. I think that I was called. I think that it was a telephone conversation at 2.00 in the morning, because I know that I was outside the command what I was called, and I came to the command and we had that conversation. However, I cannot remember now what the circumstances were and what year, but I do remember that this was at 2.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You're not even able to help us at all with whether it was at the beginning of the war, the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot. But the specific time when the conversation took place helped me to remember that the conversation had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 26 of your statement in this case, which is D614, you state: "I was personally present as a liaison officer at a large number of meetings between General Mladic and UNPROFOR representatives." Are you able to provide anything more specific of that statement, approximately how many meetings or how frequent these meetings were? Are you able to provide us any further information about that?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: There were - and once again we're approximating here - but let's say that there were at least five such meetings because in the attempt to enable the process of creating conditions for a cease of hostilities, military workgroups were formed which dealt with questions of cease-fires. So when an agreement was achieved at a lower level, then the commanders of the warring parties would come to verify the agreement and sign it. For example, this was the case --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll discuss the specifics --

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: -- of the demilitarisation of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We'll discuss the specifics here in a little bit. I just want to understand the dynamics before I discuss the specifics with you of certain occasions. Is it correct that you would sometimes serve as General Mladic's interpreter at meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Depending on whom he had a meeting with. If it was UNPROFOR representatives, they had their own interpreter so that my job would be to monitor the accuracy of the interpretation because in war, everything is possible and it was possible for the interpreter to deliberately misinterpret. If he had some direct talks, I could also serve as an interpreter. I don't remember if there were such cases with General Mladic. I remember I once or a couple of times worked for General Tolimir as an interpreter. But I'm not sure if I was ever the only interpreter for General Mladic. I think it did happen once at Borike near Rogatica [Realtime transcript read in error "Plitvice"].

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In the Galic case at transcript page 18667, you were asked the following: "Q. Would you please answer the question. "A. I acted as interpreter at the meetings that General Mladic attended. "Q. Yes. And that's between September 1992 and August 1994, is that correct, including that period?" Your answer was: "Yes. "Q. How often?" Your next answer: "On several occasions when these meetings were held. Perhaps on five occasions." Do you stand by your previous evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: It's the same as I -- as what I said now. But let me say about my previous answer that it was mis-recorded. Borike is not near Plitvice. It's near Rogatica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. And I see that you corrected that. Prior to a meeting, is it correct that General Mladic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Witness, you said that your testimony today is the same as what you said then. Today you testified that, as far as you remember, you once acted in Borike as the interpreter for General Mladic. The previous testimony says that your estimate was it may have been some five times that you did so. So it's not the same. I just wanted to draw your attention to that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I just explained that it's also a duty of the interpreter to monitor the interpretation provided by a person brought by General Rose, General Smith, or somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This is a more precise answer. And when in the Galic case you said it happened five times, that included those occasions where you did not interpret but where you verified the accuracy of the interpretation of the other interpreters present. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Prior to a meeting, is it correct that General Mladic would usually ask as much as possible about the person with whom he was supposed to have a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. And that's perfectly natural because at all meetings everybody tries to get as much background on their collocutors as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During these meetings, is it correct that you would also have additional private conversations with General Mladic in the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "private conversations," but we certainly did speak to each other in Serbian. I cannot understand from your question what would be private or not private.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, just during the course of the meetings you would have conversations between the two of you in Serbian that were not translate -- being translated to the group as a whole; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Probably. Probably. But I don't know what's at issue here. What needed to be interpreted was interpreted. Perhaps the General asked after my wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, that's not really what I'm asking about. It's -- did you have conversations about what was being discussed at the meetings with General Mladic in Serbian during the course of the meetings? So I'm not talking about random how is your family stuff, but would you -- would the two of you discuss the substance or the topics of what the meeting was about to yourselves during the course of the meetings?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I cannot say anything specific, but we probably did because General Mladic, as an outstanding commander, always liked to hear the opinions and suggestions of his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And when you attended meetings with other members of the Main Staff, whether it was General Milovanovic or General Tolimir, would you also have conversations with them prior to the meeting and also -- well, prior to the meeting about the person or the matter that you were to be meeting about?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I would rather say yes than no. I can't remember specifically but I think so, because it would be only natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to now turn into some specific matters. Do you agree that it is improper to block a medical evacuation of critically ill civilian patients from leaving Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I agree. Not only from Sarajevo but anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31181 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, appearing before you is an article dated 23 November 1993 from the French Press Agency in Paris entitled: "Bosnia Serbs Block Medical Evacuation." In the article it states: "A 24-year-old Bosnian Serb with a serious chest wound from a sniper's bullet was amongst those who would die unless they were flown out of Sarajevo, said Peter Kessler, spokesperson for the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Refugees." The next paragraph describes an interaction with a Serb official at Lukavica barracks about the convoy, and in the following part of the article it states: "He said 'let him die,' said Kessler, quoting the response of the Serb liaison officer Milenko Indjic to his description of the man's medical condition." Do you recall this incident?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: This is pure rubbish. And I see you are showing me an AFP article. And I have to say, as I said in the previous trial, if you are going to base your conclusions on newspaper stories, you are talking to a dead man right now because the Sarajevo paper Oslobodjenje had published in 1992 news that I was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So in answer to my question are you saying you don't recall this incident because it did not happen in your view?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that I don't remember. I'm saying that this is nonsense. I want you to show me the request for this convoy and a paper where it says it's rejected.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to this because of your comment. You're saying that -- you're saying, "I'm not saying that I don't remember." Do you remember a medical evacuation of critically ill individuals in November of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I remember the medical evacuation from Sarajevo to Italy of Ismet Bajramovic, known as Celo, a notorious Sarajevo criminal who harmed a lot of Serbian people, because I was personally present at this Sarajevo airport when his evacuation was approved. He had a bullet in his heart. If the evacuation of a notorious criminal was approved, then do you really believe that this story happened as presented here?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let's stick to the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What happened at another time is not the issue at this moment. Do you remember a medical evacuation where a 24-year-old Bosnian Serb with a serious chest wound was not granted in November 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember. Because if any request of that kind had been made, it would certainly have been approved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you don't remember, then this is a general statement. The witness, Mr. Weber, does not remember such an incident at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that this incident did happen and that Mr. Kessler, an individual who is -- appears to not only be seeking to evacuate a 24-year-old Bosnian Serb but was also looking to evacuate 14 patients total including two children and three women along with 17 of their relatives. I put it to you that this event did happen and Mr. Kessler has no reason to make this up. Do you have any reason to believe that he is?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you that this is a lie and that it's you who is fabricating. Show me a request for medical evacuation and I will agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I again stop you. Earlier you said you don't remember such an incident, although the question was a bit composite. Do you know Mr. Kessler?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I apologise for my emotional reaction. This claim is a personal insult to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for Mr. Kessler, I remember the name but I can't put a face to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Are you in a position to tell us whether or not Mr. Kessler would have any reason either to make things up or don't you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you remember ever to have said - and I'm not suggesting you did but I'm asking you - do you remember ever to have said that someone -- you'd rather let someone die than to let him go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I certainly never said that, and I don't remember that any medical evacuation had ever been refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I'd just tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31181 receives number P6710, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6710 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll try to squeeze in one more document before the break. Could the Prosecution please have P04624 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, before you is a 21 March 1995 UNPROFOR memorandum concerning a meeting between Colonel De Kermabon and General Milosevic at the Lukavica headquarters. According to the document, in the second page, you were present for this meeting. I just want to give you a second to orient yourself to the memorandum, and could you let us know do you recall this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I know Colonel De Kermabon very well, but somehow I can't remember that I attended this meeting nor do I see any indication of that in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: For the sake of the witness, could we have page 2 of the document so we can also look at that, also, in the B/C/S version and English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I see that I was there, but I can't recall it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go back to page 1 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In item 2 related to the security at the airport, the memo discusses that for over a week the aircraft arriving and departing at the airport were engaged by Serbian forces, including an event involving rocket fire on the 19th of March. Before I further go on, does this help your recollection at all about this meeting, this particular matter?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I can't remember. I mean, I don't rule out any of what is written here, but I really can't remember this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The memo then states: "After some discussion, General Milosevic said he would ensure that his forces around the airport refrain from firing on aircraft. This was based upon the concept that Muslims would not be on the incoming/outgoing flights." Do you recall General Milosevic not wanting Muslims either arriving or leaving Sarajevo on flights from the airport?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You have no reason to dispute that this accurately represents what General Milosevic communicated at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: No, I have no reason to dispute it, but I just have no recollection of this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we're at the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's time for a break. Mr. Indjic, would you please follow the usher. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we will resume at 25 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was going to move on to another document, but I didn't know if Your Honours have any questions on this. No. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, not as far as I'm concerned. No. Then perhaps you already ask it to be brought to our screen, unless you want the witness not to see it when he enters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31190.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Indjic, before you is a 29 June 1995 memorandum from Viktor - excuse me for the pronunciation here - Bezrouchenko --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Bezrouchenko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Greatly appreciate it as always.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: To David Holland concerning a meeting with you in Lukavica. Just like before, I'd like to give you a fair opportunity to just review the document and orient yourself and let us know if you recall this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I remember it vaguely. I remember there was a problem after the closing of the bridge at Grbavica that Colonel Bezrouchenko came.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to actually direct your attention to subsection b of the memorandum related to the BiH Army offensive. In this paragraph it relates what you said and indicates you stated: "Yesterday's attack in the area of Nedzarici was initiated by Serbs who have now adopted a new strategy. This strategy is to clench their grip of urban Sarajevo." Before continuing, do you see this passage?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Who informed you of this strategy?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember whether the term "strategy" was used in the conversation or not. The strategy as such was certainly not the subject of conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It states: "This strategy is to clench their grip of urban Sarajevo." Who communicated that to you, to clench their grip of urban Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you that strategy, in my view, did not exist, so nobody could convey that strategy to me. I can't tell you how each part of the conversation was interpreted and what we discussed specifically, but when you read the whole talk, you can see that we discussed all the combat activity and the Serb response to Muslim actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We're going to go through it, but I just want to stop part by part so we don't get too confused. How did you know the attack in the area of Nedzarici was initiated by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Probably from the meetings at the corps command or from talking to somebody from the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to the next sentence, you stated that: "The BSA is going to nibble away Bosnian positions in the city in response for every hill the Bosnians seize around Sarajevo." How were you informed that this was going to be done by the SRK?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Probably at the meetings in the corps command. That's quite natural.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to the following sentences, you said that: "UNPROFOR might see BSA tanks close to PTT very soon." And then according to the memorandum, you emphasized the importance of the battle around Sarajevo to the outcome of the war. Were these your personal opinions or statements based on instructions you were provided? You've explained to us that you had no discretion. On what basis were you saying this?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: First of all, nobody took any statements from me. That's one thing. This is a conversation between David Harland and Viktor Bezrouchenko with me. In that conversation I had the right to my own opinion, to share it or not share it. So everything I said in this conversation is what I presented. On what basis I knew that, that's a different issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The last sentence of this subsection states: "When I asked him what type of weapon was used to attack the TV building yesterday, he," in reference to you, "smiled and said that the BSA had an assortment of weapons." Is it correct that you smiled and made this statement because you knew the SRK hit the RTV building the day before, the 28th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I really cannot answer this question. I smiled a couple of times in the course of today. Whether I smiled on that day, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you said the BSA had an assortment of weapons --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Part of your question was about the smile. Second was the reason for the smile.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you further seek an answer to that portion of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Is it correct you knew that the SRK had hit the RTV building the day before, the 28th of June, 1995, when you made this statement?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I'm saying again: I didn't give any statements and nobody took any statements from me. Whether the TV building was hit or not, I cannot remember now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's an answer to the question, that you don't remember. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: According to this memorandum you said the BSA had an assortment of weapons. Is it correct that you were aware that the SRK possessed modified air bombs at the time of this meeting, on the 29th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I don't see that I mentioned modified air bombs anywhere here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it's not true that I knew.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- could you please answer the question. Irrespective of what the document says, the document talks about a variety of weapons, but were you aware of the BSA having modified air bombs at their disposal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender the document into evidence, 65 ter 31190.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 31190 receives number P6711, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have still a question in relation to this document before it disappears from the screen. Can you tell me who was present during that meeting which is mentioned in this memorandum we see on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say any more than I read in the memorandum. Harland, Bezrouchenko, and myself. I don't know if anybody else was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I don't see that in the memorandum. What is your recollection? I'm asking you for your recollection.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who was there. I can see in the memorandum that Bezrouchenko and I were there and that it is sent to Harland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I can see that as well and that is the reason why I'm asking you. You said earlier, this is on page 71, line 7 and 8: "This is a conversation between David Harland and Viktor Bezrouchenko with me." That is what you said. When I'm looking at this memorandum, it shows that Bezrouchenko sent this memo to Mr. Harland [Realtime transcript read in error "Bezrouchenko"], mentioning in the first line: "This morning I," referring to Mr. Bezrouchenko, "had a meeting with Lieutenant-Colonel Indjic in Lukavica." Do you recall any meeting you had directly with Mr. Bezrouchenko in the absence of Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely correct, Your Honour. I made a mistake. This is evidently a meeting of Bezrouchenko and myself, so I cannot say that I recall this specific meeting, but I had many meetings with him. This was not the only one. But I remember that it was a question of after the closure of closing the Bratstvo i Jedinstvo Bridge, how to resolve the problem of civilians that remained on each side. The bridge was opened for the civilians. So it's my error when I mentioned Harland. The reason why I specifically cannot say anything about this meeting with Bezrouchenko is that there were many meetings with Bezrouchenko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you recall any meeting with Mr. Bezrouchenko when you talked about hitting the TV tower?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall that meeting, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you participate in meetings related to the state commission for the exchange of prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes, only when it was necessary to organise something in the technical sense, because there was an official state commission headed by Dragan Bulajic and he dealt with all the things that had to do with exchanges.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: What were you organising in the technical sense?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Since the meetings were mostly held, as I said earlier, on neutral territory at Sarajevo airport, it was necessary to co-ordinate the time, to organise the transport, these technical details about the way in which people would get to the place of the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to make a short correction of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Page 73, line 23, I said it shows that Bezrouchenko sent this memo to Mr. Harland. This should be correct. And not Mr. Bezrouchenko. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During these meetings, is it correct that it would be discussed, locations where people were being detained?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: I say again, in principle, I did not take part in exchange negotiations in the professional sense but in the technical sense, in organising the meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Before we move on to another document, do you agree that it is improper to hold women, children, and elderly men in detention facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILENKO INDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I absolutely agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, actually for this next document, if we could go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- Mr. Weber, is it possible for -- to see what is written at the bottom of this page that is on the screen under the heading: "Corridor via Igman"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I can make it out with some difficulty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have a copy that would be clearer?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We can provide copies of the document to the Chamber, if you'd like -- or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm interested in that sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Or if the court officer could blow up the last exhibit. I believe it is P6711. And, Your Honour, I believe you were inquiring about page 1 at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: In the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which is not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did you say you don't have a clearer copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is -- it is still difficult. Not uploaded electronically. In a hard copy I can make out most of the words except probably for the fourth or fifth one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm missing --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- two words, as a matter of fact. I think that all the rest is --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- legible. What I see is that the previous lines ends with "to cut a corridor along this," and then there is two words where the second may be something of defence, the first one I have difficulties in reading, and then it continues: "... will meet fierce and determined resistance of the BSA ..." That seems to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I believe that -- Ms. Stewart informs me - I can see on her screen also - that if it's made just the English version and it's blown up, that bottom portion specifically, even more than this, that the full sentence may be legible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My staff member, who is always of great assistance, suggested that it could read: "Along this route by force will meet fierce and determined resistance..." If the parties could agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's what I'm reading on Ms. Stewart's screen right now, so do I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any dispute about this last line, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We just wanted to check, Your Honours, because we do have the B/C/S translation, so we wanted to see if that corresponds to the original and then we will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- state our position on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The proper order is the other way around - that is, to check in the original whether the translation is accurate or not. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I asked if we could move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Indjic, whatever you have heard or seen in private session is confidential. You should not only now but never share that information with anyone else. That is an order by this Court. And heavy penalties can be imposed if you violate such an order. I also instruct you, but that's separate from what I just said, that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether you gave it today or whether it's still to be given tomorrow. And we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. By the way, this -- the first order I gave you is without any time-limit. It's valid forever. The instruction I gave you as far as discussing your testimony is a different one and that will extend up to the moment where you have finally concluded your -- giving your evidence. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30 in this same courtroom. You may now follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 3rd of September, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, II.
